docs.title: The product
docs.text:
What is AlgoBridge?

AlgoBridge keeps Salesforce objects and PostgreSQL tables in step, in both directions. Changes in Salesforce are copied to your tables. Rows you insert, update or delete in a read-write table are sent back to Salesforce. Your application works with plain SQL and never calls the Salesforce API itself.

It does the job of a hosted Salesforce sync service, but you run it yourself as one container image, next to your own PostgreSQL, with no licence fee and no per-row charge.

Is it really free?

Yes. AlgoBridge is open source and self-hosted. You can run it in production without paying anyone. If you want help, CloudAlgo offers paid consulting and support: book a consultation or see Pricing.

Is AlgoBridge released?

Not yet. Version 2 is in active development. The core of the sync is built in both directions, but some features, such as alerts screens, webhooks and the API, are still to come. See Release notes for what exists today.

How is it different from a hosted sync service?

The main differences:

  • Cost. Hosted sync services are usually priced by the number of rows you sync. AlgoBridge has no licence fee and no per-row charge; you pay only for the container and database you already run.
  • Hosting. You run AlgoBridge on your own infrastructure, on any platform that runs containers, rather than on one vendor's platform.
  • Your data stays with you. Sync state lives in a PostgreSQL database you own, not in someone else's service.
  • API limits. Some hosted services make calls that do not count toward your org's API limits. AlgoBridge's calls do, like any integration you run yourself, so it is built to spend as few as possible. See API budget.
  • Change detection from Salesforce. AlgoBridge polls with SOQL, cheaply, or uses an optional notifier that Salesforce calls when records change.
  • Licence. AlgoBridge is open source.

Pricing sets these side by side.

docs.title: Setup and running
docs.text:
What do I need to run it?

Three things: a container runtime that keeps the container running, PostgreSQL 15 or later, and outbound HTTPS to Salesforce. AlgoBridge needs no Redis, message broker or shared disk. See Install.

Does AlgoBridge need its own database?

Yes. AlgoBridge keeps its own data, such as users, mappings, jobs and watermarks, in a database of its own. Your synced tables live in your client database. The two must be different databases, though they can share a PostgreSQL server. AlgoBridge refuses to use its own database as the client database. See Architecture.

Can one instance sync several Salesforce orgs or databases?

No. One instance syncs exactly one Salesforce org with exactly one client database. To sync another pair, run another instance. This keeps every setting, job and alert unambiguous.

Can I run more than one container?

Yes. The same image runs as APP_ROLE=web (console only), worker (sync only) or all (both). Workers coordinate through PostgreSQL, so you can run several and any one can take over from another. See Workers and jobs.

What does AlgoBridge change in my database?

It creates your mapped tables and a small set of objects in one schema, algobridge by default: a change log, its archive, a capture trigger on each read-write table, and a few status columns. Everything it creates carries the algobridge_ prefix. It never drops or recreates a table, and every schema change is shown to you as a diff before you apply it. See Client database.

docs.title: Sync behaviour
docs.text:
How does AlgoBridge learn about changes in Salesforce?

By polling with SOQL, in two steps. A cheap probe first asks whether an object has changed since the last pass. Only if it has does AlgoBridge fetch the changed records. You can also install an Apex bundle that answers the probe for up to 90 objects in one call. Or you can use the change notifier, which lets Salesforce tell AlgoBridge which objects changed at no API cost. See Change sources.

Does AlgoBridge use Change Data Capture or streaming events?

No. Salesforce Change Data Capture is not used at all. Detection is SOQL polling, optionally sped up by the change notifier, and a daily reconciliation sweep catches anything polling misses.

How quickly do changes appear?

From PostgreSQL to Salesforce, a change is sent when 200 changes are waiting, or when the oldest has waited the maximum wait: 60 seconds by default, adjustable from 10 to 900. From Salesforce to PostgreSQL, it depends on the poll interval: 5 minutes by default for a busy object, backing off to 30 minutes for a quiet one. With the change notifier, a fetch starts as soon as Salesforce sends its notification. The governor slows everything down if your org's API usage gets high.

How many Salesforce API calls will it use?

It depends on how many objects you map, how often they change, and which change source you use. As a guide, detection for 50 objects polled every 5 minutes costs about 2,900 calls a day with the default Composite probe, about 290 with the Apex probe, and about 25 with the change notifier. Fetches and writes come on top. API budget shows how to estimate your own total.

What happens if both sides change the same record?

Each read-write mapping has a conflict policy: sf_wins (the default), pg_wins or latest_wins. A conflict exists only while a PostgreSQL change for the record is still waiting to be sent. See Conflicts.

What happens when Salesforce rejects a change?

AlgoBridge retries it, with growing delays, up to 5 times. If it still fails, the change is parked as failed and shown on the Activity screen with Salesforce's error message. From there you can retry it or discard it. A failure on one record holds back only that record and any children that refer to it; everything else keeps syncing. See PostgreSQL to Salesforce.

Are formula fields synced?

No. Salesforce does not update a record's SystemModstamp when only a formula's inputs change, so polling could never keep a formula value correct. The mapping editor shows formula fields as not synced.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Does any of my data leave my network?

Only what Salesforce sync needs: AlgoBridge calls Salesforce for the objects and fields you map. If you use the change notifier, Salesforce sends AlgoBridge object names, never record data. If you configure SMTP, invitation and reset emails go through your mail server. AlgoBridge sends no telemetry. See Security.

How do people sign in?

With a local email and password, optionally with two-step verification, or through single sign-on with Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra ID or any OpenID Connect provider. Access is invite-only by default, and there are three roles: viewer, member and admin. See Single sign-on and Users and roles.

docs.title: Pricing
docs.text: AlgoBridge is free. It is open source and self-hosted. You can run it in production, on as many instances as you need, without a fee or a licence key.

docs.title: Self-hosting is free
docs.text:
Self-hosted Licence open source Cost of the software none Instances as many as you run What you provide a container runtime, PostgreSQL 15 or later, outbound HTTPS to Salesforce What you pay for your own infrastructure, and the Salesforce API calls AlgoBridge makes against your org's existing allowance

Your running costs are your own hosting, plus the API calls AlgoBridge spends from your org's existing daily allowance. There is no per-record or per-row charge. To estimate the API usage, see API budget.

docs.title: Compared with a hosted sync service
docs.text:
AlgoBridge A typical hosted sync service Cost No licence fee and no per-row charge. You pay for your own container and database. Usually priced by the number of rows synced, so the bill grows with your data. Hosting Self-hosted. One container image you run on any platform that runs long-lived containers, next to your own PostgreSQL. Runs on the vendor's platform, and your database usually has to live there too. Where sync state lives In a PostgreSQL database you own. In the vendor's service. Salesforce API limits Every call counts against your org's API request limit, so AlgoBridge batches every read and write and runs a budget governor. Varies; some services' calls do not count toward your limits. Licence Open source. A commercial service. Change detection in PostgreSQL A trigger on each read-write table records changes in a change log. Usually a trigger and log as well. Change detection in Salesforce SOQL polling, through a cheap probe, with an optional Apex probe or change notifier. Varies by service. Conflicts sf_wins, pg_wins or latest_wins, set per mapping. Often no conflict policy setting. A failed insert with ordered writes Holds back only that record and its children. Can hold the whole queue.

The API limit is the trade-off

Running AlgoBridge yourself costs you no licence fee and no per-row charge, but its Salesforce calls come out of your org's daily allowance. How large a share depends on what you map and how often it changes; see the worked example in API budget.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text:
AlgoBridge v2 is in development

Version 2 has not been released yet. It is a ground-up redesign, and the features below are built and tested but not yet published as a release. Some features are still to come; see Still to come. Expect changes before the first release.

This page lists what has been built so far, in the order it was built, newest first. Dates are when the work joined the main branch.

docs.title: Change notifier
docs.text:
2026-10-06

  • Push notifications from Salesforce. Record-triggered Flows tell AlgoBridge which objects changed, so it learns about changes without spending API calls. Notifications carry object names only, never record data. See Change notifier.
  • One-click pairing between the instance and the org, at a cost of 2 API calls, with key rotation and an instant revoke.
  • Signed requests. Every notification is signed and checked for key, org, timestamp, replay and rate. Repeated failed requests open an alert.
  • A slow fallback poll, hourly by default, catches anything a notification missed.
  • Your own saves are ignored. Changes made by AlgoBridge's integration user do not trigger notifications, so synced writes are not echoed back.
  • Fair to your org. The notifier leaves 1% of the org's daily asynchronous Apex allowance untouched.

In this version you add the Flows by hand; see Apex bundle.

docs.title: Apex probe and change sources
docs.text:
2026-10-05

  • The Apex bundle. A small, read-only Apex package you can deploy to your org from the console. It answers "has anything changed?" for up to 90 objects in one API call, against 5 per call without it.
  • Choose your change source: Composite (the default, nothing to install), Apex probe or change notifier. AlgoBridge verifies your choice before saving it, re-checks it daily, and falls back with an alert if it stops working. See Change sources.

docs.title: Live log
docs.text:
2026-10-03

  • A real-time view of every process's log lines in the console, for administrators. Follow, pause, filter and copy. Nothing is stored; the log streams only while someone is watching. See Live log.
  • Clearer SSO refusals. When an identity provider refuses a sign-in, the log now records the provider's error code.

docs.title: Initial load, Reload and the daily sweep
docs.text:
2026-09-25

  • Initial load of every record when you activate a mapping, over REST or Bulk API, whichever costs fewer calls, with progress on the console.
  • Reload empties a table and loads it again. You confirm it by typing the table name.
  • Daily reconciliation sweep removes rows Salesforce no longer has and repairs rows that differ. It refuses to delete a large share of a table at once.
  • Outbound sends on a latency bound: a batch goes when 200 changes are waiting or the oldest has waited the maximum wait.
  • Formula fields are blocked from sync, because polling cannot keep them correct.

docs.title: API budget governor and adaptive intervals
docs.text:
2026-09-21

  • Soft and hard thresholds for the org's API usage. Above the soft threshold AlgoBridge slows down; above the hard threshold it pauses Salesforce calls, while changes keep queuing. See API budget.
  • Adaptive poll intervals. A quiet object is polled less often, and a busy one returns to its minimum interval.

docs.title: Salesforce to PostgreSQL sync
docs.text:
2026-09-21

  • Change probes that check 5 objects per API call before reading anything.
  • Fetch and apply of changed records, matched on sfid and then on External ID, including deletes.
  • Conflict policies per mapping: sf_wins, pg_wins and latest_wins. See Conflicts.

docs.title: PostgreSQL to Salesforce sync, Bulk API and Activity
docs.text:
2026-09-21

  • Writes to Salesforce over SOAP, 200 records per call, sending only changed fields, with the new sfid written back to your row.
  • Bulk API v2 for runs of 2,000 records or more.
  • Retries with backoff for rejected changes; failures are parked rather than lost.
  • The Activity screen: every change in both directions, with filters, record detail and Salesforce's error text. Retry or discard a failed change, or retry all failures.

docs.title: Provisioning
docs.text:
2026-09-19

  • Tables built for you. AlgoBridge creates and extends mapped tables, the change log and the capture trigger in your database.
  • Additive changes only. It never drops or recreates a table, and it refuses a change that would narrow a column.
  • You stay in control. Every change is shown as a diff and runs only when you press Apply. A preflight check names any missing database grant.

docs.title: Mappings
docs.text:
2026-09-18

  • Map Salesforce objects to tables: choose fields, set direction (read-only or read-write), pick an External ID, add reference fields.
  • Choose a write algorithm: Ordered or Merged.

docs.title: Job runner
docs.text:
2026-09-15

  • Background jobs coordinated entirely in PostgreSQL, with a worker registry, automatic takeover when a worker stops, and a watchdog that restarts stalled schedules.
  • The Jobs and workers screen. See Workers and jobs.

docs.title: Salesforce connection
docs.text:
2026-09-15

  • Connect your org through an External Client App, using OAuth with PKCE against your My Domain. Tokens are stored encrypted.
  • API usage at a glance. The connection screen shows the org's API usage and AlgoBridge's own share. See Salesforce connection.

docs.title: Client database connection
docs.text:
2026-09-14

  • Connect your PostgreSQL from the console or with CLIENT_DATABASE_URL. The connection string is stored encrypted. See Client database.
  • Encrypted secrets with key rotation, through the rotate-encryption-key command.
  • A setup checklist on the dashboard.

docs.title: Single sign-on, form protection and user management
docs.text:
2026-09-14

  • Single sign-on through OpenID Connect, with presets for Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID and a generic option for other providers. Optional sign-up by email domain, and a setting to require SSO. See Single sign-on.
  • Every form is protected by a signed token and a one-time key, so forged and double submissions are refused.
  • User management: invitations, role changes, disabling users and admin-issued password-reset links, with optional email over SMTP. See Users and roles.

docs.title: Foundation, sign-in and console shell
docs.text:
2026-09-13

  • One container image that runs as console, worker or both, with health endpoints and a migrate command.
  • Local sign-in with argon2id passwords, optional two-step verification and account lockout.
  • Three roles (viewer, member, admin), with every route denied unless it names the permission it needs.
  • The console shell and the create-admin command for the first administrator.

docs.title: Still to come
docs.text:
Planned, and not in the current build:

  • Automatic notifier Flows and a daily check of them, plus mutual TLS and an IP allow-list for the notify endpoint.
  • Alerts on their own screen and by email.
  • Webhooks for sync events.
  • A REST API (/api/v1) with access tokens.
  • An audit log of console actions.
  • A settings screen for instance settings.

Before the first release, single sign-on will be checked against real Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID tenants, and the Apex bundle will be checked in a clean Salesforce org.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
These pages explain how AlgoBridge works and why it works that way. Read them before you plan a production rollout. They cover the decisions that affect your Salesforce API usage, your database and your security review.

Page What it covers Architecture One container image, the three process roles, and why PostgreSQL does all the coordination. What AlgoBridge stores in its own database and what it adds to yours. Salesforce to PostgreSQL How changes made in Salesforce are detected, fetched and applied to your tables. Change notifier The optional push path: Salesforce tells AlgoBridge which objects changed, at no API cost. PostgreSQL to Salesforce How a row you write in PostgreSQL is captured, batched and sent to Salesforce, and what happens when Salesforce rejects it. API budget Why AlgoBridge counts against your org's API limits, how the governor protects them, and how to estimate your daily calls. Conflicts What counts as a conflict, and the three policies for resolving one. Security Sign-in, roles, form protection, secret encryption, request signing, and which data leaves your network.

New to AlgoBridge?

Start with Architecture, then read API budget. The budget page explains the design choice that matters most: how AlgoBridge spends your org's API calls.

docs.title: API budget
docs.text: Every call AlgoBridge makes to Salesforce counts against your org's API request limit. That is true of any integration you run yourself, and it shapes the whole design. This page explains the limit, how AlgoBridge keeps within it, and how to estimate what your instance will use.

docs.title: Why every call counts
docs.text:
Salesforce limits how many API requests an org can make in a rolling 24 hours. An Enterprise Edition org gets 100,000 requests plus 1,000 per user licence. REST, SOAP, Bulk API and Bulk API 2.0 requests all count. Your other integrations share the same allowance.

Some hosted sync services have calls that do not count toward your API request limits. That exemption is not open to software you run yourself. AlgoBridge pays for every call, the same as any other integration in your org, and in return you get no per-row charge and a sync that runs on your own infrastructure.

So AlgoBridge treats call efficiency as a requirement, not a tuning option:

  • Never one call per record. Reads come in pages of 2,000 records, or as Bulk API jobs. Writes go 200 records per SOAP call, or as Bulk API jobs for large runs.
  • Cheap when nothing changes. A probe asks whether an object has changed before anything is read. See Salesforce to PostgreSQL.
  • The cheaper transport wins. Loads and sends compare the call cost of each transport and pick the lower one.
  • A governor watches the total. It slows and then pauses AlgoBridge before your org runs out.

docs.title: Watching usage at no cost
docs.text: Salesforce reports the org's current usage on every REST response, in the Sforce-Limit-Info header, and in the limit information returned with SOAP responses. AlgoBridge reads it from responses it was getting anyway, so tracking usage costs nothing. It also counts its own calls by the hour, so the connection screen can show the org's total use and AlgoBridge's share of it.

docs.title: The governor
docs.text:
The governor compares the org's usage with two thresholds you set as instance settings.

Org usage State What happens below the soft threshold normal Nothing changes. at or above soft (sf_api_soft_percent, default 70%) slowed Every mapping's poll interval is multiplied by 4, capped at one hour. The outbound maximum wait is multiplied by 4. The daily sweep is deferred. An API budget alert opens. at or above hard (sf_api_hard_percent, default 90%) paused Probes, fetches, writes to Salesforce and new Bulk jobs all wait. The alert escalates. back below soft minus 5 points normal Scheduling resumes and the alert closes.

A few rules make the governor safe to rely on:

  • Capture never pauses. Changes in PostgreSQL keep queuing in the change log while writes are paused, so a pause costs latency, never data.
  • The 5-point margin stops flapping. Without it, an org sitting right on the threshold would open and close the alert on every pass.
  • Recovery is automatic. A paused instance moves back to slowed as soon as usage drops below the hard threshold. While paused, AlgoBridge refreshes its usage reading every 10 minutes, so it notices the drop.
  • It fails open. Before AlgoBridge has a usage reading, it runs normally rather than blocking.
  • Loads check headroom first. An initial load or Reload weighs its estimated cost against the remaining headroom before it starts.

Choosing thresholds

The thresholds are a share of the whole org's allowance, not of AlgoBridge's own use. If other integrations already use most of your limit, lower the soft threshold so AlgoBridge backs off before they are affected.

Open the governor states full size

docs.title: Adaptive intervals
docs.text: Each mapping polls on its own interval, between a minimum (default 5 minutes, allowed 2 to 60) and a maximum (default 30 minutes). After 3 empty probes in a row the interval doubles. A change resets it to the minimum. A busy object stays near the minimum; a quiet one settles at the maximum and costs few calls. The console shows each mapping's current interval and why it last changed.

docs.title: What change detection costs
docs.text:
The cost of finding changes depends on the change source. These figures are for 50 mapped objects.

Change source Calls per poll Calls/day at a 2-minute interval Calls/day at 5 minutes Range across intervals One query per object (not used; for comparison) 50 36,000 — — Composite probe (default) 10 (5 objects per call) 7,200 about 2,900 about 480 to 7,200 Apex probe 1 (up to 90 objects) 720 about 290 about 48 to 720 Change notifier 0 per change — — about 25 a day: an hourly fallback poll plus 1 daily check

On top of detection, each change source pays for:

  • Fetches. About 1 call per 2,000 changed records, and at least 1 call for each object a probe finds changed.
  • The daily check that your change source still works: 1 call a day.
  • The daily sweep. One Bulk query per mapping, about 5 calls per mapping per day.

The Change notifier page breaks down its costs in full.

docs.title: Estimating your calls per day
docs.text:
Add up five parts:

Part How to estimate it Detection (objects ÷ objects per call, rounded up) × polls per day. Polls per day = 86,400 ÷ the interval in seconds. Fetch For each poll that finds changes: changed objects × (changed records ÷ 2,000, rounded up). Sweep 5 × mapped objects. Change-source check 1. Writes to Salesforce For each read-write mapping: changed rows ÷ 200, rounded up, per send. Each send is at least 1 call, and a mapping sends at most once per maximum wait (60 seconds by default) unless 200 changes are waiting. Runs of 2,000 or more go through Bulk API at about 6 calls each.

One-off work, such as initial loads and Reloads, comes on top. A REST load costs about 1 call per 2,000 records. A Bulk load costs about 5 calls plus 1 per 50,000 records. AlgoBridge picks the cheaper one.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The figures below are arithmetic from stated assumptions, not measurements.

Assumptions. An Enterprise Edition org with 100 user licences, so the limit is 100,000 + 100 × 1,000 = 200,000 calls a day. 50 mapped objects on the Composite probe. All 50 stay busy enough to poll at the 5-minute minimum all day (the worst case for detection). Each poll finds changes in 10 objects, each with fewer than 2,000 changed records. 5 of the mappings are read-write, and each sends one SOAP batch a minute, around the clock.

Part Arithmetic Calls/day Detection 10 calls per poll × 288 polls 2,880 Fetch 10 objects × 1 call × 288 polls 2,880 Sweep 5 × 50 250 Change-source check 1 Writes to Salesforce 5 mappings × 1,440 sends 7,200 Total 13,211

That is about 6.6% of the org's allowance, well under the 70% soft threshold.

Two changes would cut it sharply. Installing the Apex bundle brings detection down from 2,880 to 288 calls. In practice, quiet objects back off toward the 30-minute maximum, so real detection and fetch costs are usually lower than this worst case.

Your numbers

The connection screen shows the org's actual usage and AlgoBridge's share. After a day of real traffic, trust those figures over any estimate. See Salesforce connection and Change sources.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
AlgoBridge is one container image. It talks to two PostgreSQL databases and one Salesforce org. It has no message broker, no cache and no shared disk. This page explains how those parts fit together and why the design is so small.

Open the architecture diagram full size

docs.title: One instance, one sync pair
docs.text:
An instance syncs exactly one Salesforce org with exactly one client PostgreSQL database. There are no workspaces and no tenants. If you need to sync a second org or a second database, run a second instance.

This keeps the product easy to reason about. Every setting, every job and every alert on an instance belongs to the same pair, and you never have to ask which connection a row belongs to.

docs.title: One image, three roles
docs.text:
The same image runs in any of three roles. You choose the role with the APP_ROLE environment variable.

APP_ROLE Serves the console Runs sync jobs Typical use all (default) yes yes A single container. Good for most installs. web yes no Scale the console separately from the sync work. worker no yes Run sync work away from the public endpoint.

A fourth mode applies the database migrations and exits. Run it with docker run <image> migrate, or set MIGRATE_ON_BOOT=true to have the container migrate before it starts. A web or worker process refuses to boot against a database whose schema is behind its build. It tells you to run the migration first instead of starting in a broken state.

Each process exposes /healthz (the process is alive) and /readyz (it can reach its database and is ready for traffic).

See Workers and jobs for running several workers.

docs.title: All coordination happens in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
AlgoBridge has no Redis, no message broker and no external queue. Jobs, locks, schedules and the worker registry all live in PostgreSQL. The job engine keeps its tables in the algobridge_jobs schema of AlgoBridge's own database. No process holds coordination state in memory.

This has three practical results:

  • Nothing extra to run. You operate PostgreSQL and a container. There is no second stateful service to back up, patch or monitor.
  • Workers are interchangeable. Any worker can pick up any job. If a worker dies, another one takes over its work in about 20 seconds.
  • Restarts are safe. On a normal stop, a worker finishes in-flight work for up to 30 seconds before it exits. Give your container runtime a stop grace period of 45 seconds so the drain can complete.

Each mapping runs on a short self-rescheduling tick of about 10 seconds. A watchdog checks every minute and restarts any mapping whose tick chain has broken. A tick that fails 5 times in a row is set aside as a dead job, so it cannot loop forever.

docs.title: Two databases, two owners
docs.text:
AlgoBridge uses two PostgreSQL databases. They must be different databases. They may share a server.

AlgoBridge's own database Your client database Owned by AlgoBridge You Set by DATABASE_URL the console, or CLIENT_DATABASE_URL Holds users and sessions, the Salesforce connection, mappings, jobs and the worker registry, sync runs, alerts, idempotency keys, instance settings, poll watermarks, notifier keys your mapped tables and the small set of objects AlgoBridge needs to capture your changes Schema changes migrations shipped with each release only additive changes you approve in the console

The split exists so that AlgoBridge's bookkeeping never mixes with your data. You can grant AlgoBridge narrow rights on your database, back the two up on different schedules, and remove AlgoBridge without leaving product tables among your own.

AlgoBridge enforces the split. It refuses to use its own database as the client database, and the migration refuses to run against a database that already holds AlgoBridge's change log. No transaction ever spans both databases.

docs.title: What AlgoBridge adds to your database
docs.text:
Everything AlgoBridge creates in your database lives in one schema, algobridge by default, and carries the algobridge_ prefix. The prefix keeps its objects distinct from yours and from any other sync tool on the same database.

Object Purpose Your mapped tables One table per mapped Salesforce object, with a unique index on sfid and, where you choose one, on the External ID column. hstore extension Stores each captured change as old and new key-value pairs. algobridge_change_log The queue of changes waiting to go to Salesforce. algobridge_change_log_archive Sent changes, kept for 30 days for the Activity screen. algobridge_capture_change() and the algobridge_capture trigger Records every insert, update and delete on a read-write table. algobridge_lastop, algobridge_err, algobridge_id columns On read-write tables only: the row's last sync state, its last error, and a stable row identity.

Read-only mappings get no trigger and no status columns.

Schema changes are additive only

AlgoBridge never drops or recreates one of your tables. It adds columns and indexes; it never narrows a column type. When you remove a field from a mapping, its column stays. Every change is shown to you as a diff and runs only when you press Apply. Before it runs, a preflight check names any database grant that is missing. See Client database.

TRUNCATE is not captured

Row triggers do not fire on TRUNCATE, so a truncated table is not synced to Salesforce. Use DELETE when you want removals to reach Salesforce.

docs.title: Runs anywhere a container runs
docs.text:
AlgoBridge is built to be provider-agnostic. It needs three things:

  1. A long-lived container runtime.
  2. PostgreSQL 15 or later.
  3. Outbound HTTPS to Salesforce.

Beyond that it makes no assumptions about where it runs:

  • Secrets arrive as environment variables.
  • All state lives in PostgreSQL, so the container needs no local disk.
  • Logs go to standard output.
  • TLS ends at your reverse proxy or load balancer.
  • Sign-in is local accounts or any OpenID Connect provider.
  • Email, when you want it, is plain SMTP.
  • The application code calls no cloud-provider SDK.

The image is built for more than one CPU architecture.

Scale-to-zero platforms

AlgoBridge runs scheduled work, so it must stay running. On a platform that scales idle containers to zero, set the minimum instance count to at least 1.

Next: Salesforce to PostgreSQL, or go straight to Install.

docs.title: The change notifier
docs.text:
When a record is saved in Salesforce, a small Apex bundle tells your AlgoBridge instance which object changed. The instance then fetches the changed rows with one batched SOQL query and writes them to PostgreSQL. Learning about the change costs no Salesforce API calls, and an hourly fallback poll catches any notification that gets lost.

This page explains how that works. To set it up, follow Install the Apex bundle. To compare the notifier with polling, see Change sources.

When Step What happens Once Pair The operator clicks Pair. The org and the instance swap a signing key in 2 API calls. Once per object Add Flows A save Flow and a delete Flow are added for each notified object. Every save Notify The Flow queues a signed POST that carries object names only. This costs 0 API calls. Per burst of notifications Fetch One SOQL fetch per mapping pulls every row changed since the watermark into PostgreSQL.

docs.text:
The left region is what gets installed in your org. The right region is the AlgoBridge container behind its TLS proxy. Bold lines are the path a save takes. Red lines carry a signature or a certificate. Dashed lines are reads or one-off setup.

Open the system map full size

docs.title: What gets installed in your org
docs.text:
You deploy the bundle once from the Connections screen. Every name in it starts with algobridge_, so nothing in it can collide with anything else in your org.

Resource Kind What it does algobridge_Status Apex REST Reports the bundle version, whether the org is paired, the endpoint, and who paired it. The console calls it after pairing and in the daily check. algobridge_ChangeProbe Apex REST Answers one question for many objects in a single call: has anything changed since this time? The fallback poll uses it, so 50 objects cost 1 call, not 50. algobridge_NotifierPair Apex REST Takes the one-time pairing code from the console, redeems it with the instance, and stores the key it receives. algobridge_NotifyChange Invocable action Called by the Flows. It removes duplicate object names, skips saves it should not report, checks the async limits, and queues the send. It catches every error, so it can never fail a user's save. algobridge_Notifier @future callout Signs the list of object names and posts it to the instance. It uses a 10-second timeout, never retries, never follows redirects, and presents a client certificate when one is configured. algobridge_Notifier__c Custom setting (hierarchy) Holds the instance endpoint, key id, signing secret, org id, the pairing user and an optional client certificate name. Only NotifierPair writes it. algobridge_Integration Permission set Grants the classes to the integration user that AlgoBridge connects as. algobridge_Instance Remote site setting Lets Apex call your instance's HTTPS host. It is set to your instance URL at deploy time.

Each Apex class ships with its own test class.

For every synced object, two record-triggered Flows call NotifyChange:

Flow Runs Why algobridge_notify_<object>_<hash>_save After save Fires on create and update. algobridge_notify_<object>_<hash>_delete Before delete Fires on delete. It has to run before the delete, because the record no longer exists afterwards.

The hash is six characters derived from the object's API name. It keeps long names unique within Salesforce's 80-character limit for Flow names.

Adding the Flows

Today you add the Flows by hand, following the recipe in Install the Apex bundle. A coming release adds a background job that deploys and removes them for you. It is described below.

docs.title: Pairing: one click, two calls
docs.text:
Open the pairing sequence full size

  1. The console opens a pairing slot. Clicking Pair writes a one-time code to AlgoBridge's database. If the round trip hasn't finished within 3 minutes, the code stops working.
  2. The console calls the org once. It sends POST /services/apexrest/algobridge/v1/notifier/pair with the code and the instance's notify URL, plus the client certificate name when mutual TLS is on. This is the first of the two Salesforce calls.
  3. Apex calls the instance back. NotifierPair sends {code, orgId, apexVersion} to /notify/v1/pair. The instance redeems the code once, generates a key, encrypts the secret with AES-GCM, pins the key to the org id, and returns {keyId, secret, notifyUrl}.
  4. Apex stores the key and answers. The key goes into algobridge_Notifier__c with the user who paired. The console receives {paired, keyId, pairedBy}, and one status call confirms it. That is the second Salesforce call.

Why the org calls the instance

The secret never passes through your browser or clipboard, and the instance learns the org id from the org itself. Pairing again rotates the key, and the old key stops working straight away.

docs.title: A record save, end to end
docs.text:
Open the save sequence full size

  1. The Flow fires inside the user's transaction. The save Flow or the delete Flow calls algobridge_NotifyChange.notify, passing only the object name. Record data never leaves the org on this path.

  2. NotifyChange decides whether to send. It skips the send when:

    • the save came from the integration user. That is AlgoBridge writing PostgreSQL changes back, and reporting it would echo the change.
    • the org isn't paired.
    • the code is already running in a future or batch context, where Salesforce doesn't allow another @future call.
    • the transaction has used up its future-call limit.
    • the org is within the last 1% of its daily async Apex allowance. That last 1% is left for your own automation.

    Otherwise it queues one @future call per transaction, carrying the object names with duplicates removed. It catches every exception, so the save always commits. 3. Notifier signs and posts after the commit. The callout builds the body and signs it with HMAC-SHA256 over a canonical string. The request has a 10-second timeout and is never retried or redirected. 4. The instance checks the request, cheapest check first. The first check that fails rejects the request, so the expensive checks run only once the cheap ones have passed. 5. One fetch per mapping. For each mapping on a named object, the instance queues one sf-fetch job and answers {accepted, ignored}. Only one fetch job per mapping can be waiting at a time. A bulk load of 10,000 records sends many notifications, but they collapse into a single fetch. 6. SOQL since the watermark, then upsert. The fetch runs under the API budget governor. It reads every row changed since the mapping's watermark in REST query pages, and applies them 500 rows at a time. It upserts the rows into your PostgreSQL by sfid, then moves the watermark forward.
