docs.title: Safety nets
docs.text:
A notification is a hint to fetch now, not the data itself. If one is lost, the sync is delayed but never wrong, because each of these nets catches up on its own.

What happens What catches it Cost The instance is down, or a callout times out The hourly fallback poll. It runs on the hour, so all notified mappings share one ChangeProbe call and fetch only the objects that changed. The interval is sf_notifier_fallback_seconds, 3600 by default. 1 call an hour An admin deactivates or deletes one of the Flows The daily check: one status call and one Flow listing. Drift shows on the mapping's chip. AlgoBridge never turns a Flow back on against an admin's decision. 2 calls a day The key is rotated, or the org is paired somewhere else Requests signed with the old key fail check 2 and are refused. The fallback poll keeps data flowing until the org is paired again. 0 The org is close to its daily async Apex allowance NotifyChange stops queueing at the 1% reserve, and the fallback poll takes over. 0 A delete or an edit slips past everything The nightly reconciliation sweep compares ids and catches it. Already budgeted

docs.title: What change detection costs
docs.text:
AlgoBridge counts against your org's daily API limit, so every way of detecting changes has a price in calls per day. These figures are for 50 synced objects. Fetching the changed rows costs the same whichever way a change was detected, so it isn't included.

Detection How Calls a day Composite polling Ask every object for changes on the adaptive interval about 480 to 7,200 Apex probe polling One ChangeProbe call covers all 50 objects about 48 to 720 Notifier Saves push object names, plus the hourly fallback probe and the daily check 0 + 24 + 2 One-off setup Pairing (2 calls), and the Flow deploy once the Flows job ships (at most 8 per object) up to 402, once

docs.title: Planned: the Flows job
docs.text:
Coming in a later release

This section describes behaviour that is still being built. It may change before release.

Open the Flows job diagram full size

Whenever a mapping is turned on or off, or the notifier is paired, a background job runs for each affected object. Only one job runs per object at a time, so two triggers for the same object never race. Each run:

  1. Plans. It lists the object's existing Flows (1 call). It wants a Flow pair if the mapping is on, and nothing if it is off.
  2. Retires a hand-made Flow. It deactivates any Flow added by hand from the recipe, so the object doesn't notify twice (up to 2 calls).
  3. Deploys or removes the pair. It makes one Metadata API deploy and polls it about 3 times. When the mapping is off, the same step removes the Flows and the chip reads removed.
  4. Reads back and activates. It reads what was deployed (1 call) and switches on any of its Flows that are still inactive (up to 2 calls). If the org refuses, the chip reads inactive · activate in Setup and the job doesn't fail.

That is at most 8 calls per object, spent once. For 50 objects that is at most 400 calls, and the governor spreads them out. While the governor has paused spending, the job waits and runs later. A configuration problem, such as a missing permission, marks the job failed without retrying. A temporary failure retries. Either way, the mapping keeps syncing on the hourly fallback poll.

docs.title: Planned: hardening the notify endpoint
docs.text:
Two optional layers are planned for locked-down deployments. Both sit on top of the request signature, and neither replaces it.

Mutual TLS You upload a client certificate to Salesforce and name it during pairing. The Notifier presents it on every send. Your reverse proxy verifies the certificate and forwards its fingerprint in a header. AlgoBridge trusts that header only on requests that come from an address in TRUSTED_PROXIES, so a client can't forge it by sending the header itself. Source allow-list You choose a verified source: a list of Salesforce egress address ranges. AlgoBridge refuses requests from any other address.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
A conflict happens when the same record changes in Salesforce and in PostgreSQL before either change has reached the other side. This page explains exactly when AlgoBridge treats a change as a conflict, and the three policies you can choose for resolving one.

Conflicts only arise on read-write mappings. A read-only mapping never writes to Salesforce, so its table simply follows Salesforce.

docs.title: When is it a conflict?
docs.text:
"Both sides changed" has a narrow and exact meaning in AlgoBridge. A conflict exists only while the change log holds an unsent PostgreSQL change for the record, that is, a change still in the NEW or CLAIMED state, at the moment a Salesforce change for the same record arrives.

Anything else is not a conflict:

  • A PostgreSQL change that has already been sent and accepted is settled. A later Salesforce change is simply applied.
  • A Salesforce change that has already been applied is settled. A later PostgreSQL change is simply sent.

AlgoBridge makes the decision inside the inbound apply transaction, after it has locked the affected rows. An edit you commit while the batch is waiting for its locks is still seen. An edit that comes after waits for the batch to finish. So there is no window in which a change slips past the check.

docs.title: The three policies
docs.text:
You set the policy per mapping in the mapping editor. A read-write mapping must have one; the editor defaults to sf_wins.

Policy What the incoming Salesforce change does What the pending PostgreSQL change does sf_wins (default) Applied to your row. Still sent afterwards. pg_wins Skipped this pass. Your row is left exactly as it is. Sent as normal. latest_wins Applied if Salesforce's change is the same age or newer; skipped if it is older. Sent as normal.

The policy only decides what happens to the incoming Salesforce change. It never cancels a pending PostgreSQL change.

docs.title: sf_wins
docs.text:
Salesforce's version of the record is written to your table at once. Your pending change is still sent afterwards. Updates send only the fields you changed, so Salesforce ends up holding your values for those fields, and its own values everywhere else. The next poll brings that combined record back to PostgreSQL.

Choose this when PostgreSQL should always reflect Salesforce as soon as possible, and your own edits are expected to go through.

docs.title: pg_wins
docs.text:
The incoming Salesforce change is skipped for this pass, and your row keeps your edit. The watermark still moves past the record, so AlgoBridge does not read it again and again. Your change is then sent. That send gives the record a new SystemModstamp, so the next poll fetches it and brings back the combined record.

Choose this when PostgreSQL is the system where edits matter most, and you never want an incoming change to overwrite a row with a send still pending.

docs.title: latest_wins
docs.text:
AlgoBridge compares two timestamps:

  • the record's SystemModstamp in Salesforce, and
  • the time your newest unsent change to the record was captured in PostgreSQL.

If the Salesforce change is newer, it is applied as with sf_wins. If your change is newer, the Salesforce change is skipped as with pg_wins. Ties go to Salesforce. Salesforce timestamps are accurate only to the second, and re-applying a record costs nothing, while dropping one could lose an edit.

Clock accuracy

latest_wins compares a timestamp taken by Salesforce with one taken by your database, so it is only as good as your database server's clock. sf_wins and pg_wins do not depend on clocks at all.

docs.title: Loads and the sweep always side with Salesforce
docs.text:
The conflict policy applies to day-to-day polling. Two jobs follow fixed rules instead:

  • Reload empties the table and loads it again from Salesforce.
  • The daily reconciliation sweep overwrites rows that differ from Salesforce with Salesforce's values. It skips any row that still has a change waiting to be sent. That pending change then goes out and settles the record in the normal way.

See Salesforce to PostgreSQL for both.

docs.title: Why a policy matters
docs.text:
Many sync tools have no conflict setting and simply call their sync eventually consistent, so which edit survives is left to timing. AlgoBridge offers the three policies above per mapping, and the default, sf_wins, gives a predictable result for most installs.

See Mappings to set a mapping's policy.

docs.title: PostgreSQL to Salesforce
docs.text:
This page explains how a row you insert, update or delete in PostgreSQL reaches Salesforce. It applies to mappings set to read-write. Read-only mappings never write to Salesforce.

The path has four steps:

  1. Capture. A trigger on your table records the change in a log, inside your own transaction.
  2. Batch. Changes wait briefly so they can be sent together.
  3. Send. A batch goes to Salesforce over SOAP or Bulk API v2, whichever costs fewer calls.
  4. Write back. Salesforce's answer, including the new record Id, is written to your row.

Open the PostgreSQL to Salesforce data flow full size

docs.title: Capture: a trigger and a change log
docs.text:
When you activate a read-write mapping, AlgoBridge adds a trigger named algobridge_capture to its table. The trigger runs before every insert, update and delete, for each row. It writes the row's old and new values, as hstore, to algobridge_change_log, and it sets the row's algobridge_lastop column to PENDING.

Because the trigger runs inside your transaction, capture is exact. A change is logged only if your transaction commits, and a rollback leaves nothing behind. Your application keeps writing plain SQL. It needs no client library and makes no API call.

Capture never stops. Even when the API budget governor pauses sending, the trigger keeps logging, so nothing is lost while Salesforce is out of reach.

What the trigger cannot see

A trigger captures only the writes that fire it. Three things bypass it, and changes made that way never reach Salesforce:

  • TRUNCATE, which fires no row trigger. Use DELETE when you want removals to reach Salesforce.
  • Disabling the trigger with ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER.
  • A session with session_replication_role = replica, which skips ordinary triggers.

docs.title: Batching: size and maximum wait
docs.text:
Sending one change per API call would quickly exhaust your org's limits. So AlgoBridge waits for changes to accumulate, within a bound you control.

Every mapping checks its queue on a tick of about 10 seconds. The check reads PostgreSQL only and costs no Salesforce call. A send starts when either of these is true:

  • 200 changes are waiting. That fills one SOAP call.
  • The oldest change has waited longer than the maximum wait. The default is 60 seconds, adjustable from 10 to 900 seconds with outbound_max_wait_seconds.

So a busy table sends full batches quickly, and a quiet table sends a single change within about a minute. While the governor has slowed the instance, the maximum wait is multiplied by 4.

A send claims up to 10,000 waiting changes at once. Claims use SKIP LOCKED, so two workers never take the same row. Within a mapping, changes are claimed strictly in capture order.

docs.title: Choosing the transport: SOAP or Bulk API v2
docs.text:
AlgoBridge picks the transport by estimated call cost.

SOAP Bulk API v2 Records per call up to 200 a job, any size Cost 1 call per 200 records about 6 calls per job Used when runs under 2,000 records, and always for Merged writes runs of 2,000 or more of the same action, Ordered writes only Answers at once asynchronously

A Bulk job's fixed overhead makes it more expensive than SOAP below about 1,200 records. Switching at 2,000 leaves a clear margin. A Bulk insert also needs the mapping's External ID field so results can be matched back to rows. Without one, the run simply stays on SOAP.

Updates send only the fields that changed. A field you set to NULL is sent as a cleared field. Inserts send every writable field.

docs.title: Ordered and Merged writes
docs.text:
The instance's write algorithm controls how several changes to the same record are sent.

Ordered (default) Merged Several changes to one record Sent one by one, in order Folded before sending: an insert plus updates becomes one insert, several updates become one update with the latest values Transport SOAP, or Bulk for large runs SOAP only

Ordered is the safe choice for most installs. Merged saves calls when the same records are updated many times between sends.

docs.title: Parents before children
docs.text: If a row refers to a parent record that has not reached Salesforce yet, the row is held back until the parent is inserted. Only that record and its children wait; everything else keeps syncing, where some sync tools stop the whole queue behind one failed insert.

docs.title: Write-back and echo suppression
docs.text:
The Salesforce call runs between two short database transactions, so no lock on your table is held while AlgoBridge waits on the network.

When Salesforce answers, AlgoBridge writes back to each row: the new sfid for an insert, the system fields, and the sync state in algobridge_lastop and algobridge_err. The sent changes move to algobridge_change_log_archive in the same transaction. They stay there for 30 days for the Activity screen.

The write-back runs under SET LOCAL ab.in_sync = true. The capture trigger sees that setting and does not log these writes. Without it, writing the sfid back would itself look like a new change and be sent again. The setting is local to the transaction, so your own sessions are never affected.

docs.title: When Salesforce says no
docs.text:
Each change in the log has a state.

State Meaning NEW Waiting to be sent. CLAIMED Taken by a send in progress. DONE Accepted by Salesforce. MERGED Folded into another change by Merged writes. DEAD Failed for good; needs your decision. DISCARDED You chose to drop it.

docs.title: Transient failures are retried
docs.text:
A rejection from Salesforce is always retried, because it is often temporary: a locked record, a validation rule someone is about to fix, or a missing parent. Each change gets 5 attempts. The delay grows from 60 seconds and doubles each time, capped at one hour, with random jitter so retries do not arrive in step. A change that keeps failing reaches DEAD after about 15 minutes.

If a worker stops in the middle of a send, its claimed changes return to NEW after 21 minutes and are sent again. Inserts go as upserts on the External ID where the mapping has one, so a resent insert updates the record the first attempt created instead of making a duplicate.

docs.title: Permanent failures stop at once
docs.text: Some changes can never be sent, whatever Salesforce says. An example is a row whose value cannot be converted to the field's type. AlgoBridge marks these DEAD straight away rather than wasting calls on retries.

docs.title: Dead changes stay visible
docs.text:
A DEAD change stays in the live log. It is not silently dropped. On the Activity screen you can retry or discard one change, or retry every failed change at once.

Error text never reaches the logs

Salesforce's error messages can quote the field values you sent. AlgoBridge stores the error with the change and shows it only on the Activity screen, behind sign-in. It never writes it to a log line.

See Mappings to make a mapping read-write, and Live log to watch sends as they happen.

docs.title: Salesforce to PostgreSQL
docs.text:
This page explains how a change made in Salesforce reaches your PostgreSQL table. Each mapped object goes through the same three steps:

  1. Detect. Find out cheaply whether the object has changed since the last pass.
  2. Fetch. Read only the changed records, in large pages.
  3. Apply. Write them to your table in one transaction, matched on sfid.

AlgoBridge detects changes by polling with SOQL, or by being told about them by the optional change notifier. It does not use Salesforce Change Data Capture or streaming events.

Open the Salesforce to PostgreSQL sequence full size

docs.title: Why polling, and why it is cheap
docs.text: Every call AlgoBridge makes counts against your org's daily API limit (see API budget). So the design goal is simple: never spend a call per record, and spend as few calls as possible when nothing has changed. In most orgs, most objects are unchanged most of the time. A cheap "has anything changed?" check, followed by a full read only when the answer is yes, uses far fewer calls than reading every object on a timer.

docs.title: Watermarks
docs.text:
AlgoBridge keeps a watermark for each mapping in its own database. The watermark is the SystemModstamp of the newest record it has applied. Every detect and fetch asks for records at or after that stamp.

The watermark is deliberately cautious:

  • It only moves after the apply commits. It advances to the highest stamp actually written to your table. A crash mid-fetch repeats some work; it never skips a record.
  • It uses >=, not >. SOQL timestamps have one-second resolution, so several records can share a stamp. Re-reading the boundary second is cheap and safe, because the apply is idempotent.
  • It stays 120 seconds behind the present. A record saved in a long Salesforce transaction can appear with a stamp slightly in the past. Holding the watermark back by two minutes keeps such records from being missed.
  • A long gap triggers a full fetch. If a watermark is more than 14 days old, AlgoBridge treats the mapping as out of date and fetches it in full. Salesforce keeps deleted records in the recycle bin for 15 days, so a shorter gap still sees every deletion.

docs.title: Detecting changes: probes
docs.text:
A probe asks one question per object: has any record changed since the watermark? A singleton probe job runs once a minute and checks every mapping that is due. You choose how the probe is answered. This choice is the instance's change source.

Change source How it asks Objects per call Needs Composite (default) One queryAll of SELECT Id … WHERE SystemModstamp >= <watermark> LIMIT 1 per object, bundled into one Composite request 5 nothing extra Apex probe One call to the AlgoBridge Apex class, which runs the same check for each object inside Salesforce 90 the Apex bundle installed in the org Change notifier Salesforce posts the names of changed objects to AlgoBridge 0 per change the Apex bundle, Flows on each object, and a reachable AlgoBridge URL

The Composite probe uses queryAll so that deleted records count as changes too.

The Apex probe class is read-only. It runs with sharing and in user mode, so it sees only what the integration user may see. It never returns record data, only which objects have changed.

docs.title: Choosing and keeping a change source
docs.text:
You pick the change source on the console. AlgoBridge checks that the source works, with one status call, before it saves your choice. After that it re-checks once a day at 02:20 UTC, at a cost of 1 call.

If your chosen source stops working, for example because someone removed the Apex class, AlgoBridge falls back to the next one that still works. The notifier falls back to the Apex probe if it is verified, and otherwise to Composite. At the same time it opens an alert. Your selection is never changed for you. Once you fix the cause, the next check restores your chosen source. See Change sources.

docs.title: The change notifier, in short
docs.text:
With the notifier, two record-triggered Flows on each object call an Apex action when a record is saved. The action sends AlgoBridge one signed POST /notify/v1/changes naming the objects that changed. It never sends record data. Salesforce's outbound callouts do not count as API requests, so detection costs nothing per change. AlgoBridge then fetches the changes as usual.

The notifier is a fast path, not the only path. Flows do not fire in every case (undelete and merge, for example). A slow fallback poll, hourly by default, and the daily sweep catch anything a notification missed. The Change notifier page covers pairing, the request checks, the safety nets and the costs in full.

docs.title: Adaptive intervals
docs.text:
Each mapping has its own probe interval, and AlgoBridge adjusts it to how busy the object is:

  • It starts at the minimum interval: 300 seconds by default, adjustable from 120 to 3600 seconds.
  • After 3 empty probes in a row, the interval doubles, up to the maximum interval (1800 seconds by default).
  • As soon as a probe finds a change, the interval drops back to the minimum.
  • If Salesforce rejects one object's probe, only that mapping backs off. The others in the same call carry on.

A busy object is checked often. A quiet one costs a few calls an hour. When the API budget governor slows the instance down, all intervals stretch further.

docs.title: Fetching changed records
docs.text:
When a probe reports a change, AlgoBridge reads the changed records with one queryAll. The query selects the mapped fields plus IsDeleted, ordered by SystemModstamp ascending. Salesforce returns up to 2,000 records per page, and each page is one API call. Records are applied in batches of 500.

Formula fields are never synced. Their values change without changing SystemModstamp, so polling could never keep them correct. Leaving them out is more honest than syncing values that silently go stale.

docs.title: Applying records: upsert on sfid
docs.text:
Each batch is applied to your table in one transaction:

  1. Deletes first. Records Salesforce reports as deleted are removed by sfid.
  2. Match on External ID. If the mapping has an External ID field, a row with the same External ID and no sfid yet is updated and gains its sfid. This links rows you inserted in PostgreSQL before Salesforce assigned an Id.
  3. Upsert on sfid. Every live record is then inserted, or updated where a row with the same Salesforce Id already exists.

If one row cannot be written, for example because a value breaks one of your constraints, that row is skipped and counted. The rest of the batch still commits. One bad row never blocks a whole object.

docs.title: Echo suppression
docs.text:
The apply runs under SET LOCAL ab.in_sync = true. The capture trigger on your table sees that setting and does not record these writes as new changes. Without it, every record AlgoBridge pulled from Salesforce would be sent straight back. The setting is local to the transaction, so it can never leak into your own sessions.

When a record has also changed on the PostgreSQL side, the apply follows the mapping's conflict policy.

docs.title: Initial load, reload and the daily sweep
docs.text:
Polling handles day-to-day changes. Three other jobs keep a table complete:

  • Initial load. When you activate a mapping, AlgoBridge counts the records and loads them all. It picks whichever transport costs fewer calls: REST queries at about one call per 2,000 records, or a Bulk API query at about 5 calls plus one per 50,000 records. When the load ends, the watermark is set to the moment it started, so changes made during the load are picked up next.
  • Reload. Empties the table and loads it again from Salesforce. Because it erases data, you confirm it by typing the table name.
  • Daily reconciliation sweep. Once a day, by default at 03:00 UTC, one Bulk query reads every mapped field of every record, at about 5 calls per mapping. The sweep removes rows Salesforce no longer has and fixes rows that differ, with Salesforce's value winning. It catches what polling cannot, such as records purged from the recycle bin before a poll saw them. It skips rows with a change still waiting to go out, and it refuses to delete a large share of a table at once. It waits while the governor has slowed or paused the instance.

See Mappings for activating, reloading and sweeping a mapping, and Live log to watch these passes as they run.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: AlgoBridge holds credentials for your Salesforce org and your database, and it can change records in both. This page explains how it protects them: who can sign in, what each role can do, how every change is protected against forgery and double submission, how stored secrets are encrypted, and what data leaves your network.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text:
AlgoBridge supports two ways to sign in. You can use both at once.

Local accounts. Email and password, with optional two-step verification (TOTP). Passwords are hashed with argon2id. The first administrator is created from the command line with create-admin. Local accounts also serve as a break-glass route if your identity provider is unavailable.

Single sign-on. One OpenID Connect adapter, with presets for Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID, and a generic option for any other OIDC provider. Several providers can be active at the same time. See Single sign-on.

A few rules apply to every sign-in:

  • Identities are keyed by issuer and subject, never by email. Changing an email address at your provider cannot hand an account to someone else.
  • Invite-only by default. A person needs an invitation before they can sign in. To allow self sign-up through single sign-on, list your email domains in AUTH_ALLOWED_DOMAINS. A person with a verified email in one of those domains is created on first sign-in, as a viewer.
  • You decide who may use a password. AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN is all (the default), admins (only administrators may sign in with a password) or off (single sign-on only).
Limit Value Session lifetime 12 hours, absolute Idle timeout 2 hours Failed attempts before lockout 5 Lockout 15 minutes Invite and password-reset links single use, valid for 7 days A started SSO sign-in must finish within 10 minutes

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
AlgoBridge has three roles. Permissions are defined in code, not edited in the console, so a role means the same thing on every instance.

Role Can Viewer See sync status and errors. Member Everything a viewer can, plus retry failed records, operate sync, and create, edit and delete mappings. Admin Everything, including managing connections, users and settings, and viewing the Live log.

Every route is denied unless it names the permission it needs, so a new screen cannot ship open by accident. AlgoBridge also refuses to remove or demote the last administrator. See Users and roles.

docs.title: Every write is forgery-checked and idempotent
docs.text:
Every form that changes something carries two hidden values:

  • A signed form token (_csrf) proves the form came from AlgoBridge, for this session. The token is an HMAC-SHA256 signature, using a key stored in AlgoBridge's database, and it is bound to your session. A forged or missing token is refused. Scripts send it in the Algobridge-Form-Token header.
  • A one-time idempotency key (_idem) is issued fresh each time a form is shown. If the same form is submitted twice, for example by a double click or a browser retry, the action runs once.

How a repeated submission is answered:

Case Answer The first submission redirected The same redirect is sent again. Nothing runs twice. The first submission rendered a page 409. A rendered page may show a one-time secret, so it is never replayed. The first submission is still running 409. Same key, different form contents 422.

Idempotency keys expire after 24 hours.

Serve AlgoBridge over HTTPS

Over HTTPS, AlgoBridge's cookies carry the __Host- prefix, which locks them to your exact origin. AlgoBridge refuses to start with a plain http:// PUBLIC_URL, unless the URL is on loopback or you set ALLOW_INSECURE_PUBLIC_URL=true. Use that setting only for local testing.

docs.title: Encryption of stored secrets
docs.text:
Secrets AlgoBridge stores in its database are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under the key in ENCRYPTION_KEY (32 bytes, base64). This covers:

  • the client database connection string,
  • the Salesforce tokens and connected app secret,
  • the change notifier's secrets,
  • two-step verification keys.

Each value records which key encrypted it, so AlgoBridge can tell old keys from new.

docs.title: Rotating the key
docs.text:
1. Set the new key in ENCRYPTION_KEY and the old one in ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS.
  2. Run the rotate-encryption-key command. It re-encrypts every stored secret under the new key in one transaction.
  3. Remove ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS.

See Configuration.

Keep the key safe

Without ENCRYPTION_KEY, the stored secrets cannot be decrypted. Store it in your secret manager or platform configuration, never in the image or in source control.

docs.title: The Salesforce connection
docs.text: AlgoBridge connects to Salesforce through an External Client App that you create in your org, using OAuth with PKCE. It connects only to your org's My Domain (*.my.salesforce.com). Disconnecting revokes the token in Salesforce. Use a dedicated integration user, so you control exactly what AlgoBridge can see and change. See Salesforce connection.

docs.title: Notifier request signing
docs.text:
When you use the change notifier, Salesforce sends requests to AlgoBridge. Every request is signed with HMAC-SHA256 under a secret shared at pairing. AlgoBridge checks the key, the signature, the org, a timestamp within five minutes and a nonce it has not seen before. It also limits body size, the number of object names and the request rate. A refused request gets an empty answer, so a caller learns nothing about why it failed. Repeated refusals open an alert.

A notification carries only object API names, never record data. The worst a stolen secret allows is triggering early fetches, which the governor still bounds. The Change notifier page lists every check and covers key rotation and revocation.

docs.title: What data leaves your network
docs.text:
Traffic Direction What it carries Salesforce API calls outbound HTTPS Queries and writes for the objects and fields you map. Change notifications inbound, from your Salesforce org Object API names only, and only if you use the notifier. Email outbound SMTP Invitation and password-reset links, and only if you configure SMTP. Without SMTP, the links are shown to the administrator instead.

Nothing else leaves. AlgoBridge has no telemetry and makes no calls to its maintainers.

Logs go to standard output and never carry field values or Salesforce error text. Salesforce error messages can quote the values you sent, so they are stored with the change and shown only on the authenticated Activity screen.

docs.title: Not yet built
docs.text:
These features are planned and are not in the current build:

  • mutual TLS and an IP allow-list for the notifier endpoint,
  • an audit log of console actions,
  • the /api/v1 API and its access tokens,
  • outgoing webhooks.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This section takes you from nothing to a first synced table. You install AlgoBridge, create the first admin, connect both ends of the sync pair, and watch the first records arrive.

docs.title: What AlgoBridge is
docs.text:
AlgoBridge is open-source, self-hosted Salesforce sync, with no licence fee and no per-row charge. It keeps a Salesforce org and a PostgreSQL database in sync in both directions:

  • Salesforce to PostgreSQL. AlgoBridge learns which objects changed, either by polling with SOQL on a schedule or from the optional change notifier in your org, then fetches the changed records and upserts them into PostgreSQL tables it creates and owns.
  • PostgreSQL to Salesforce. For mappings you make read-write, a row-level trigger captures every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE into a change log table, and AlgoBridge sends the changes to Salesforce in batches.

A few properties shape how you deploy it:

Property What it means for you One container image The same image serves the console and runs the sync work. APP_ROLE decides which a container does. Single tenant You run your own instance, on your own infrastructure, with your own data. There is no hosted service. One sync pair per instance An instance syncs exactly one Salesforce org with one PostgreSQL database. For another pair, run another instance. PostgreSQL only Jobs, sessions and all state live in PostgreSQL. There is no Redis, broker or external queue. Counts against your API limits Like any integration you run yourself, AlgoBridge spends your org's API requests. Every read and write is batched, and polling slows down or pauses on its own as the org nears its limit. See API budget.

AlgoBridge does not use Salesforce Change Data Capture or any streaming API.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Before you start, have these ready:

You need Why Notes A long-lived container runtime Runs the AlgoBridge image. Docker Compose, Kubernetes, or any platform that keeps a container running. The worker must stay on: scale-to-zero platforms need a minimum of one instance. PostgreSQL 15 or later, for AlgoBridge itself The platform database: users, connections, mappings, jobs and sync state. Set as DATABASE_URL. The reference Compose file runs one for you. A PostgreSQL database for your application data The client database: the tables AlgoBridge syncs. Must be a different database from the platform database. They may share a server. AlgoBridge refuses to connect its own database as the client database. A Salesforce org and an External Client App in it AlgoBridge signs in to the org through this app with OAuth. You create the app in Salesforce Setup during your first sync. A dedicated integration user is recommended. Outbound HTTPS AlgoBridge calls Salesforce's APIs. Inbound HTTPS from Salesforce is only needed for the optional change notifier. A public address for the console Sign-in redirects and the Salesforce callback are built from it. Set as PUBLIC_URL. It must be https:// unless the host is localhost. Terminate TLS at your reverse proxy or platform.

Two databases, always

AlgoBridge keeps its own data and your data apart. The platform database holds the algobridge_jobs schema and the algobridge_migrations table. The client database holds your mapped tables, the capture triggers and the algobridge_change_log table. No transaction ever spans both.

docs.title: The path to a first sync
docs.text:
1. Install AlgoBridge. Start the image and its platform database with Docker Compose, set PUBLIC_URL and ENCRYPTION_KEY, and check that /readyz answers.
  2. Create the first admin. Run create-admin, open the set-password link it prints, and sign in.
  3. Connect both ends. On the Connections screen, connect your client database and your Salesforce org.
  4. Add a mapping and provision it. Choose a Salesforce object, choose its fields, then click Create table. AlgoBridge creates the table in PostgreSQL and starts the initial load.
  5. Watch it sync. Follow the initial load on the mapping's Load panel and in the Live log.

When the first sync works, the configuration reference lists every environment variable the app reads.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Architecture explains the web and worker roles and how they coordinate through PostgreSQL.
  • Change sources compares the three ways AlgoBridge can learn about Salesforce changes, and what each costs.
  • Single sign-on adds Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra ID or a generic OIDC provider.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
This page lists every environment variable AlgoBridge reads, with its default and what it does. Use it when you write your Compose file, Kubernetes manifest or platform config.

AlgoBridge reads its configuration only from environment variables. It never calls a secrets-manager API: if your secrets live in one, have your platform inject them as environment variables.

docs.title: How configuration is checked
docs.text:
All settings are parsed once at start, against one schema. If anything is wrong, the process exits before it serves a request, with one line that names every problem:

Invalid configuration — DATABASE_URL: must be a postgres:// connection string; SMTP_URL and SMTP_FROM must be set together

A few rules apply throughout:

  • An empty value counts as unset for every optional variable, so SMTP_URL= is the same as leaving it out.
  • Lists are comma-separated. Spaces around items are trimmed, items are lowercased, and duplicates are dropped.
  • Some variables come in sets. Setting only part of a set, such as SMTP_URL without SMTP_FROM, is refused.
  • Set the same environment on every container. Web and worker containers read the same variables, and the migrate, create-admin and rotate-encryption-key commands read them too.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
Variable Default Required Meaning APP_ROLE all No What the container runs: all (console and jobs), web (console only) or worker (jobs only). See APP_ROLE. PORT 3000 No The HTTP port every role listens on, including worker, for its health checks. An integer from 1 to 65535. PUBLIC_URL http://localhost:3000 Yes, outside a local trial The address people reach the console at, such as https://sync.example.com. Must be a bare http(s) origin with no path, query or fragment. Must be https:// unless the host is localhost, *.localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]. Sign-in redirects, the Salesforce callback and the change notifier's endpoint are built from it, and requests from other origins are rejected. ALLOW_INSECURE_PUBLIC_URL unset No true accepts a plain http:// PUBLIC_URL on a non-local host, for example on an isolated network. Session cookies can only be locked to the host over https, so use this only on a network you trust. LOG_LEVEL info No The lowest level written to stdout: fatal, error, warn, info, debug or trace. Opening the Live log raises it to debug for the Live log only, never for stdout. MIGRATE_ON_BOOT unset No true makes the container's serve command run the platform database migrations before it starts the app. Read by the image's entrypoint, not by the app. Convenient for a single container; with several containers, run migrate as a separate step. BUILD_COMMIT set at build time No The git commit the image was built from, shown shortened in the sidebar footer. A 7 to 40 character hex SHA. Normally passed as the BUILD_COMMIT build argument rather than set at run time.

The image also sets NODE_ENV=production. You don't need to change it.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Variable Default Required Meaning DATABASE_URL none Yes The platform database: AlgoBridge's own users, connections, mappings, jobs and sync state. A postgres:// or postgresql:// URL. PostgreSQL 15 or later. CLIENT_DATABASE_URL unset No The client database, the one AlgoBridge syncs. When set, it wins over a connection saved on the Connections screen, and the screen refuses to save or disconnect. See below for the format.

CLIENT_DATABASE_URL is checked at start with the same rules the Connections screen uses. It must:

  • start with postgres:// or postgresql://;
  • include a host, a user name, and exactly one database name after the host;
  • carry no query option other than sslmode, which must be one of disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full.
CLIENT_DATABASE_URL: postgres://app_user:change-me@db.example.com:5432/app?sslmode=require

It must point at a different database from DATABASE_URL. A URL that points at the platform database is refused when the connection is checked.

Warning

Setting CLIENT_DATABASE_URL replaces a connection saved on the Connections screen the first time the connection is checked, and the saved URL cannot be recovered. If you unset the variable later, enter the URL in the console again.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: Variable Default Required Meaning ENCRYPTION_KEY unset Needed to connect Salesforce Encrypts the secrets AlgoBridge stores: Salesforce tokens and app credentials, a client database URL saved in the console, and two-step verification keys. Exactly 32 random bytes in base64: generate it with openssl rand -base64 32. The app starts without it, but saving a connection or turning on two-step verification is refused. ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS unset No Only while rotating keys: the old key. It still decrypts, and never encrypts. Requires ENCRYPTION_KEY, and must differ from it.

docs.title: Rotating the encryption key
docs.text:
Rotation has no downtime.

  1. Generate a new key with openssl rand -base64 32.
  2. On every container, move the current key to ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS, put the new key in ENCRYPTION_KEY, and restart.

  3. Re-encrypt every stored secret with the new key:

    docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm app rotate-encryption-key

    It prints Re-encrypted N stored secret(s) with key <id>. You can now remove ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS. It runs in one transaction: if any value cannot be decrypted, nothing changes, and the command names the problem.

  4. Remove ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS and restart.

docs.title: Salesforce
docs.text:
Variable Default Required Meaning SALESFORCE_CLIENT_ID unset No The consumer key of the External Client App AlgoBridge signs in through. SALESFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET unset No The app's consumer secret.

Set both or neither. When both are set, they win over credentials saved on the Connections screen, and the screen shows the app as Set by the deployment. When neither is set, an admin saves them on the Connections screen instead. The org itself is always connected from the console. See Salesforce connection.

docs.title: Sign-in and single sign-on
docs.text: By default, people sign in with an email and password, plus optional two-step verification. Single sign-on providers are added with AUTH_PROVIDERS; several can be active at once. See Single sign-on for the provider setup.

docs.title: General
docs.text: Variable Default Required Meaning AUTH_PROVIDERS local No Comma-separated sign-in methods: any of local, google, microsoft and oidc. Must include local unless AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN=off. Each SSO provider listed needs its own settings below. AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN all No Who may sign in with an AlgoBridge password: all, admins or off. admins is recommended once SSO works, keeping a break-glass path. off removes the password form and needs at least one SSO provider. create-admin and admin-issued set-password links work in every mode. AUTH_ALLOWED_DOMAINS empty No Comma-separated email domains, such as example.com, whose verified SSO users may sign up on first sign-in without an invite. New accounts start as viewer. When empty, every new user needs an invite.

docs.title: Google Workspace
docs.text:
Required together when AUTH_PROVIDERS includes google.

Variable Meaning GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID The OAuth client ID. GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET The OAuth client secret. GOOGLE_HOSTED_DOMAIN Your Workspace domain, such as example.com. Only accounts whose hosted domain matches it can sign in, so personal Gmail accounts are always refused.

docs.title: Microsoft Entra ID
docs.text:
Required together when AUTH_PROVIDERS includes microsoft.

Variable Meaning MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID The application (client) ID. MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET The client secret. MICROSOFT_TENANT_ID Your directory (tenant) ID, as a GUID. common, organizations and consumers are refused, because they would admit accounts from any tenant.

docs.title: Generic OIDC
docs.text:
For Okta, Keycloak, Auth0 and other standard OpenID Connect providers. The first four are required together when AUTH_PROVIDERS includes oidc.

Variable Required with oidc Meaning OIDC_ISSUER Yes The issuer URL. Must be https://. AlgoBridge reads the provider's endpoints from its discovery document. OIDC_CLIENT_ID Yes The client ID. OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET Yes The client secret. OIDC_DISPLAY_NAME Yes The provider name on the sign-in button, shown as "Continue with" followed by this name. OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS No, recommended Comma-separated email domains the provider is trusted for. Checked on every sign-in that matches by email. When empty, any verified email the provider asserts is accepted, and only the invite list keeps out unwanted accounts.

Domain lists match exactly: a subdomain of an allowed domain is not covered.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
Email is optional. Without it, invite and password-reset links are shown to the admin once, to copy and send, and alerts appear only in the console.

Variable Default Required Meaning SMTP_URL unset No The SMTP relay, as an smtp:// or smtps:// URL, for example smtps://user:change-me@mail.example.com:465. Any provider's SMTP endpoint works. SMTP_FROM unset With SMTP_URL The sender, for example AlgoBridge <noreply@example.com>.

Set both or neither.

Alert mail uses the same SMTP_URL and SMTP_FROM. It goes to every active user whose role carries alerts.receive (admins, by default), plus any extra addresses entered on the Alerts screen, which also sends a test email. The resolved mail waits until the problem has stayed clear for 15 minutes, so a problem that clears and comes straight back does not send a burst of mail.

docs.title: Jobs and workers
docs.text: No environment variable tunes the job engine. Jobs live in the algobridge_jobs schema of the platform database named by DATABASE_URL, and the only job-related setting you choose per container is APP_ROLE. Sync behaviour such as poll intervals is set per mapping in the console. See Workers and jobs.

docs.title: Demo mode
docs.text: This version reads no demo setting. A demo instance is planned as the same image with a demo flag, but the feature is not built yet.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A single-container install behind a TLS proxy, with Google sign-in and email:

environment:
  DATABASE_URL: postgres://algobridge:change-me@db:5432/algobridge
  APP_ROLE: all
  MIGRATE_ON_BOOT: "true"
  PUBLIC_URL: https://sync.example.com
  ENCRYPTION_KEY: <openssl rand -base64 32>
  SMTP_URL: smtps://user:change-me@mail.example.com:465
  SMTP_FROM: AlgoBridge <noreply@example.com>
  AUTH_PROVIDERS: local,google
  AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN: admins
  GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: change-me
  GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET: change-me
  GOOGLE_HOSTED_DOMAIN: example.com

docs.title: Run your first sync
docs.text:
In this page you connect your PostgreSQL database and your Salesforce org, map one Salesforce object to a table, and watch its records load. It follows the console's own screens in the order they ask for things.

You need a running instance with ENCRYPTION_KEY set and an admin who can sign in. If you don't have that yet, install AlgoBridge first.

Until both ends are connected, the Overview page reads Connect both ends of the pair, and the top bar shows each end as not connected. Both steps below happen on Connections, under Instance in the sidebar. Only admins see it.

Open the first sync steps full size

docs.title: 1. Connect the client database
docs.text:
The client database is your application's PostgreSQL database: the one AlgoBridge creates tables in and syncs. It must not be AlgoBridge's own platform database.

  1. Open Connections. The PostgreSQL panel reads Not connected.

  2. Paste one connection URL into Connection URL, for example:

    postgres://app_user:change-me@db.example.com:5432/app?sslmode=require

  3. Click Test and connect.

AlgoBridge connects with a 5-second timeout and runs SELECT version() before saving anything. If the test fails, nothing is saved, and the error never shows the password. Once connected, the panel lists the host, port, database, user, SSL mode and server version. The URL itself is stored encrypted and never shown again.

The URL accepts one option, sslmode (disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full). Without it the driver's default applies, which does not use SSL. Use require or verify-full for any database reached over a network.

Set it from the deployment instead

You can set CLIENT_DATABASE_URL on every container instead of using this screen. It then wins over the screen, which shows the connection as Set by the deployment (CLIENT_DATABASE_URL). See Client database for the trade-offs.

docs.title: What the database role needs
docs.text:
AlgoBridge runs every statement in your database itself; there is no "copy this SQL to your DBA" path. Before it creates anything, it checks that the role in the URL can:

  • create the hstore extension, or find it already installed;
  • own the target schema (algobridge by default), or create it.

On the first provisioning, the target schema must also be empty. When a check fails, the mapping's Apply panel names the missing grant instead of showing a raw PostgreSQL error.

docs.title: 2. Connect Salesforce
docs.text: AlgoBridge signs in to your org through an External Client App that you create in Salesforce, using OAuth with PKCE. It then acts as the Salesforce user who authorizes it. Use a dedicated integration user, so AlgoBridge's API calls and permissions stay separate from people's.

docs.title: Create the External Client App
docs.text:
1. On Connections, find the Salesforce panel and click Copy next to the callback URL. It is your PUBLIC_URL followed by /connections/salesforce/callback, for example:

    https://sync.example.com/connections/salesforce/callback

  2. In Salesforce Setup, open External Client App Manager and create a new app. Give it a name and a contact email.

  3. Turn on Enable OAuth and paste the callback URL as the Callback URL.
  4. Add the OAuth scopes Manage user data via APIs (api) and Perform requests at any time (refresh_token, offline_access).
  5. Turn on Require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE), and leave Require secret for Web Server Flow on.
  6. In the app's policies, set Refresh Token Policy to keep the token valid until revoked, or allow refresh token rotation.
  7. Save, then open Consumer Key and Secret and copy both. A new app can take a few minutes to become usable.

docs.title: Give AlgoBridge the credentials and connect
docs.text:
1. Back on Connections, paste the Consumer key and Consumer secret and click Save app credentials. The secret is stored encrypted and never shown again.
  2. Enter the org's My Domain URL, such as https://yourcompany.my.salesforce.com. A sandbox looks like https://yourcompany--sandbox.sandbox.my.salesforce.com. Only hosts ending in .my.salesforce.com are accepted.
  3. Click Connect to Salesforce. Salesforce opens.
  4. Sign in as the integration user and allow access.

Salesforce sends you back to Connections, which now shows the org, the user AlgoBridge is authorized as, and the org's API usage today.

If Salesforce shows an error What you see What to do redirect_uri_mismatch The app's Callback URL does not match the instance's. Copy it again from Connections, including https and with no trailing slash, and check PUBLIC_URL. The consumer key or secret was rejected Replace the credentials on Connections. The app must allow the refresh_token scope Add the scope to the app, wait a few minutes, and connect again. The connect link expired More than 10 minutes passed, or the link was already used. Click Connect to Salesforce again.

More cases are in Salesforce connection.

You can also supply the app's credentials as SALESFORCE_CLIENT_ID and SALESFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET. When both are set they win over the screen.

docs.title: 3. Pick a change source
docs.text:
The change source decides how AlgoBridge learns that Salesforce records changed. Fetching the changed records costs the same whichever you pick; the source decides what it costs to find out. Choose it on Connections, in the Change detection panel.

Source Installs in your org Cost to learn about changes Composite polling (default) Nothing. One API request per five objects per poll. Apex probe The AlgoBridge Apex bundle: one read-only class, its tests and a permission set. One API request per poll for up to 90 objects. Change notifier The same bundle, a one-time pairing, and two Flows per synced object. Needs AlgoBridge reachable from Salesforce over HTTPS. Zero, plus one fallback poll an hour.

For a first sync, keep Composite polling. It needs nothing installed, and you can switch later without touching your mappings.

To use the Apex probe instead:

  1. In Change detection, click Deploy bundle. The deploy runs in the background and the panel shows Deploy succeeded or Deploy failed. The integration user needs Modify All Data (or Modify Metadata Through Metadata API Functions) and Author Apex to deploy.
  2. In Salesforce Setup, assign the AlgoBridge Integration permission set (algobridge_Integration) to the integration user, and to no one else.
  3. Click Use this source on the Apex probe card. AlgoBridge makes one status call to the bundle and saves your choice only if the bundle answers.

The change notifier takes a few more steps. See Change sources and Apex bundle.

docs.title: 4. Add a mapping
docs.text: A mapping says which Salesforce object syncs into which PostgreSQL table, with which fields. Members and admins can create mappings.

docs.title: Check the instance settings first
docs.text:
Open Mappings, under Sync in the sidebar. The Settings panel holds two instance-wide choices:

  • Target schema: the PostgreSQL schema AlgoBridge creates its tables in. The default is algobridge. You can change it only until the first mapping exists.
  • Write algorithm: how changes are sent to Salesforce. Ordered Writes (recommended) is the default. Merged Writes merges several changes to one record before sending, and reorders parents ahead of children. You can change it at any time.

docs.title: Choose the object
docs.text:
1. Click New mapping. The first step, Choose object, lists the objects in your org.
  2. Search for the object, for example Account, and click Choose. Click Refresh if a new object is missing from the list.

docs.title: Choose fields and settings
docs.text:
The second step, Choose fields and settings, opens the editor. The table name comes from the object's API name, lowercased, and is fixed once the mapping exists.

Panel What to choose Direction Read-only: Salesforce changes sync to PostgreSQL, and PostgreSQL never writes back. Read-write: changes sync both ways. Read-write is unavailable for objects Salesforce reports as neither createable nor updateable. When both sides change Read-write only. Salesforce wins (the default), PostgreSQL wins, or Latest change wins. See Conflicts. Matching key An optional External ID field, chosen from fields that are External ID and Unique in Salesforce. Without one, rows inserted in PostgreSQL risk creating duplicates. Polling Fastest and Slowest poll intervals in minutes: 5 and 30 by default, each between 2 and 60. The interval stretches toward the slowest while nothing changes, and snaps back to the fastest when something does. Fields Tick the fields to sync. Id (stored as sfid) and SystemModstamp are always included, and so is IsDeleted when the object has it. CreatedDate and Name start ticked. Formula fields are listed but disabled, tagged Formula field — not synced. Reference fields Optional. Lets a child row point at its parent by the parent's External ID, for records created in PostgreSQL.

Each field becomes a column named after its API name, lowercased. Anything that blocks saving is listed under Problems and warnings.

Click Create mapping. The mapping is saved as a Draft: nothing exists in PostgreSQL yet, and nothing syncs.

Start small

For a first sync, pick an object with a modest number of records, make it Read-only, and tick only the fields you need. You can add fields later; adding a field adds its column and loads only that column.

docs.title: 5. Provision the table
docs.text:
Provisioning makes your client database match the saved mapping. It runs only when you click it.

  1. On the mapping's page, find the Apply panel. For a new mapping it reads Nothing exists in PostgreSQL for this mapping yet and lists the statements it will run.
  2. Read the statements, then click Create table.

A worker runs the plan in one transaction: if any statement fails, none of them stick, and the panel shows the failing statement. The mapping shows Provisioning while it runs, then Active.

For a read-only mapping, AlgoBridge creates:

  • the hstore extension, if it is missing;
  • the table, with sfid and one column per mapped field;
  • a unique index on sfid, a unique index on the External ID column if you chose one, and an index on each field you marked Indexed.

A read-write mapping also gets the algobridge_lastop and algobridge_err status columns, the algobridge_capture trigger on the table, and, once per schema, the algobridge_change_log table and the algobridge_capture_change() trigger function.

AlgoBridge never drops or recreates a table to apply a change. Later edits are applied the same way: save, read the pending statements on the Apply panel, then click Apply changes.

docs.title: 6. Watch the initial load
docs.text:
When a mapping first becomes active, AlgoBridge reads the whole object into the table. This is the initial load.

  1. AlgoBridge counts the object's records with one SELECT COUNT() query, then picks the cheaper transport: REST paging costs about one API call per 2,000 records; a Bulk API 2.0 query costs about five calls plus one per 50,000 records. Small objects go over REST and large ones over Bulk. If the org refuses Bulk, the load falls back to REST.
  2. The mapping's Load panel shows the load's kind (Initial load), its transport, its status and how far it has read. The Mappings list shows the same progress, for example Loading 42%.
  3. When the status reads Completed, the table holds the object's records, and normal polling takes over from the moment the load started.

If the org's API usage is near its limit, the load waits and shows Waiting for API budget rather than spending calls it cannot afford. Stop load ends a running load and keeps what it has read; Reload starts again from an empty table.

Check the result in your database:

SELECT count(*) FROM algobridge.account;

Replace algobridge with your target schema and account with your table name.

docs.title: Follow it in the Live log
docs.text:
Open Live log, under Instance in the sidebar. It streams every process's log lines to your browser as they happen, so you can watch the load's Salesforce calls and PostgreSQL writes.

  • Filter by Level (Error, Warn, Info, Debug) and by Source (Worker, Queue, SOQL, Salesforce, PostgreSQL, Web), or pick one process or one mapping.
  • While anyone has the Live log open, every process also forwards its debug lines, such as each SOQL query. Your container logs on stdout are unaffected.
  • The Live log keeps no history: lines from before you opened it are not shown. Up to five people can watch at once. Only admins can open it.

See Live log for more.

docs.title: 7. Make a change and see it arrive
docs.text:
Edit one of the synced records in Salesforce. Within one poll interval of the mapping (5 minutes by default, or longer if the interval has stretched), the change appears in the PostgreSQL row. Each pass is listed on the Activity page.

For a read-write mapping, update a row in PostgreSQL instead. The capture trigger records it in algobridge_change_log, and AlgoBridge sends it to Salesforce in its next batch: when 200 changes are waiting, or the oldest has waited 60 seconds. The row's algobridge_lastop column shows PENDING until the send settles it.

TRUNCATE is not synced

The capture trigger fires on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, row by row. A TRUNCATE changes no row as far as the trigger is concerned, so nothing is deleted in Salesforce. Use DELETE FROM <table> to remove records on both sides.

docs.title: Install AlgoBridge
docs.text: In this page you run AlgoBridge and its platform database with Docker Compose, create the first admin, and check that the instance is healthy. The same image runs on any container platform; Compose is the reference deployment.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • Docker with the Compose plugin (docker compose).
  • A copy of the AlgoBridge repository. The reference Compose file builds the image from it.
  • A host name for the console if anyone other than you will use it, such as sync.example.com, with TLS terminated in front of AlgoBridge.

docs.title: 1. Look at the reference Compose file
docs.text:
deploy/docker-compose.yml runs two services:

Service What it is db PostgreSQL 16, the platform database, with a pgdata volume and a pg_isready health check. app AlgoBridge, built from the repository's Dockerfile, listening on port 3000. It starts once db is healthy.

The app service starts with these settings:

environment:
  DATABASE_URL: postgres://algobridge:change-me@db:5432/algobridge
  APP_ROLE: all
  MIGRATE_ON_BOOT: "true"
  PUBLIC_URL: http://localhost:3000
ports: ["3000:3000"]
stop_grace_period: 45s

Everything else in the file is commented out: email, single sign-on, the client database, the encryption key and the Salesforce app credentials. The configuration reference explains each one.

docs.title: 2. Set your values
docs.text:
Edit deploy/docker-compose.yml before the first start.

  1. Change the database password. Replace change-me in both POSTGRES_PASSWORD and DATABASE_URL with the same strong password.
  2. Set PUBLIC_URL to the address people use to reach the console. Keep http://localhost:3000 for a trial on your own machine. Anywhere else it must be an https:// origin with no path, for example https://sync.example.com.

  3. Generate an encryption key and set it as ENCRYPTION_KEY:

    openssl rand -base64 32

    ENCRYPTION_KEY: <the generated value>

    AlgoBridge starts without it, but it encrypts the Salesforce tokens, stored connection URLs and two-step verification keys with it. Without it you cannot connect Salesforce, save a client database on the Connections screen, or turn on two-step verification.

Keep the key safe

Store ENCRYPTION_KEY with your other secrets. If you lose it, AlgoBridge cannot read the connections it stored, and you must connect them again. To change it later, see rotating the encryption key.

Keep secrets out of the file

For anything beyond a trial, put the passwords and keys in an .env file or your platform's secret store and reference them from Compose, rather than writing them into docker-compose.yml. AlgoBridge reads secrets only from environment variables.

docs.title: 3. Build and start
docs.text:
From the repository root:

BUILD_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD) docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml build
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

BUILD_COMMIT is optional. When set, the console's sidebar footer shows the short commit the image was built from.

On start, the container's entrypoint runs the migrations first because MIGRATE_ON_BOOT is true, then starts the app. Follow the logs while it boots:

docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml logs -f app

The migration prints applied: … (or no pending migrations) and job schema ready. Logs are structured lines on stdout.

If a setting is wrong, the container exits at once with a single line that names every problem, for example:

Invalid configuration — PUBLIC_URL: must be https unless the host is localhost (set ALLOW_INSECURE_PUBLIC_URL=true to accept plain http on a trusted network)

Fix the value and run up -d again.

docs.title: Create the first admin
docs.text:
AlgoBridge has no default account and no sign-up page. Create the first admin from the command line once the database is migrated:

docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm app create-admin --email you@example.com --name "Your Name"

The command prints:

Created admin you@example.com (invited).
Set-password link (shown once, valid 7 days): https://…
Open it to choose a password, then turn on two-factor authentication.
  1. Open the link and choose a password. The link works once and expires after 7 days.
  2. Sign in at your PUBLIC_URL.
  3. Open your Account page and turn on two-step verification. It is optional, and recommended for every admin.

If the command says Platform database is not migrated — run migrate first, run:

docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm app migrate
Lost the link, or locked out?
  • The email must not already belong to a user. If the link expired unused, run the command again with a different email, or have another admin issue a new link from the Users page.
  • If every admin is locked out, run create-admin with a new email, then issue reset links for the original accounts from Users.
  • create-admin and admin-issued set-password links work in every AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN mode, including off. They are the break-glass path when single sign-on is misconfigured.
  • Outside Docker, run node dist/cli/create-admin.js --email … --name … with DATABASE_URL and PUBLIC_URL set.

Without SMTP configured, invite and password-reset links for other users are shown to the admin once, to copy and send. To email them instead, set SMTP_URL and SMTP_FROM.

docs.title: Check health
docs.text:
The app answers two unauthenticated endpoints on PORT:

Endpoint Answers Use it for GET /healthz 200 {"status":"ok"} whenever the process is serving HTTP. Liveness. GET /readyz 200 {"status":"ready"} when the platform database answers within 2 seconds and has every migration this build expects. Otherwise 503 {"status":"unavailable"}, with "reason":"migrations_pending" when the database is behind the build. Readiness, load balancer health checks. 
curl -i http://localhost:3000/readyz

The image has its own HEALTHCHECK on /readyz: every 15 seconds, a 5-second timeout, 3 retries, and a 60-second start period that covers a migration on boot. It uses Node's own fetch, since the image has no curl or wget. docker compose ps shows the result.

docs.title: Choose an APP_ROLE
docs.text:
One image, three roles:

APP_ROLE Serves the console Runs jobs Typical use all (default) yes yes A single container. Enough for most installs. web yes no Scale the console separately, behind a load balancer. worker no yes Scale the sync work separately.

All coordination goes through the platform database, so you can run several web and several worker containers against the same DATABASE_URL. Workers share the queues, and each mapping's sync runs on one worker at a time. If a worker dies mid-job, another takes the job over, usually within 16 to 25 seconds.

Every role listens on PORT and answers /readyz. Every role needs the same environment, including ENCRYPTION_KEY.

Sync needs a running worker

With no worker or all container running, nothing syncs. The console then marks Jobs & workers with No worker is running. Sync is paused. See Workers and jobs.

docs.title: Migrations with more than one container
docs.text:
MIGRATE_ON_BOOT=true is a convenience for a single container. When you run separate roles, run migrations as an explicit one-off step instead, and leave MIGRATE_ON_BOOT unset:

docker run --rm -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://algobridge:change-me@db.example.com:5432/algobridge <image> migrate

The migration takes a database lock, so two runs at once queue rather than collide, and it is safe to run more than once. A web or worker container that starts before migrations refuses to boot with a message telling you to run migrate.

docs.title: Stopping a container
docs.text:
On SIGTERM, a worker stops taking new jobs and lets running ones finish for up to 30 seconds. Give the container more time than that, so it is never killed first:

  • Docker Compose: keep stop_grace_period: 45s from the reference file. The Compose default is 10 seconds.
  • docker stop: use docker stop --time 45.
  • Kubernetes: set terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45. The default is 30.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
1. Get the new version of the repository and build the image again.

  2. Run the migrations for the new version before any new web or worker container starts. With the reference Compose file, MIGRATE_ON_BOOT=true does this on start:

    BUILD_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD) docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml build
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

    With separate roles, run migrate as a one-off step first, then roll out the containers.

  3. Check /readyz on the new containers.

A container refuses to start against a platform database that is behind its build, with a message that lists the pending migrations. The reverse is allowed: a container older than the database starts and logs a warning, so a rollback or a rolling upgrade does not cause an outage.

A new version may also change the capture trigger AlgoBridge installs in your client database. In that case each affected mapping's Apply panel offers to reinstall change capture; nothing in your database changes until you click it.

docs.title: Install the Apex bundle
docs.text:
This guide installs the AlgoBridge Apex bundle in your org, which the Apex probe and the change notifier need. It then pairs the change notifier, adds the Flows that drive it, and checks that it works.

For how the notifier signs and checks each request, see How the change notifier works.

docs.title: What the bundle contains
docs.text:
The bundle is plain metadata, not a managed package, so you can read every line before you deploy it. Its source is in packages/salesforce/apex in the repository.

Component Purpose algobridge_ChangeProbe The Apex probe. Read-only: reports, for up to 90 objects, whether each one changed. algobridge_Status Reports the bundle version and which features are enabled. algobridge_NotifierPair Receives the one-time pairing from AlgoBridge. algobridge_NotifyChange The Flow action AlgoBridge: Notify Change. algobridge_Notifier Sends the signed notification to AlgoBridge. algobridge_Notifier__c Hierarchy custom setting that holds the notifier key. algobridge_Instance Remote site setting for your AlgoBridge address. algobridge_Integration Permission set AlgoBridge Integration. Five test classes One per class above.

The bundle is version 1.1.0. A bundle older than 1.1.0 has no notifier, and the console disables Pair notifier until you deploy again.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Salesforce is connected.
  • The integration user has Modify All Data, or Modify Metadata Through Metadata API Functions, and Author Apex. These are needed to deploy from the console.
  • For the change notifier: PUBLIC_URL is an https:// address that Salesforce can reach.

docs.title: Step 1: Deploy the bundle
docs.text:
From the consoleWith the Salesforce CLI
  1. Open Instance → Connections → Change detection.
  2. Click Deploy bundle.

The deploy runs in the background and the panel shows Deploying…, then Deploy succeeded or Deploy failed. It runs only the bundle's five test classes, and it writes the origin of your PUBLIC_URL into the remote site setting for you.

It costs one Metadata API deploy, its status polls, and one status call.

  1. Edit the remote site setting in force-app so its URL is your PUBLIC_URL origin. It ships as the placeholder https://instance.invalid. Don't commit your edit. You can also change it after the deploy in Setup → Remote Site Settings.

  2. Deploy, running only the bundle's tests:

    cd packages/salesforce/apex
sf project deploy start \
  --source-dir force-app \
  --target-org <your-org-alias> \
  --test-level RunSpecifiedTests \
  --tests algobridge_ChangeProbe_Test \
  --tests algobridge_Status_Test \
  --tests algobridge_NotifyChange_Test \
  --tests algobridge_Notifier_Test \
  --tests algobridge_NotifierPair_Test

Note

If PUBLIC_URL changes later, deploy the bundle again and pair the notifier again, so the remote site and the key match the new address.

docs.title: Step 2: Assign the permission set
docs.text:
The deploy doesn't assign the permission set.

  1. In Salesforce, open Setup → Permission Sets → AlgoBridge Integration.
  2. Click Manage Assignments and assign it to the integration user only.

The probe runs with sharing, in user mode, so it sees only what the integration user can read.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify
docs.text:
To use the Apex probe, click Use this source on the Apex probe card. AlgoBridge makes one status call and saves the source only if the bundle reports the expected version with the probe enabled. The card then shows Verified and the time.

If you only want the Apex probe, you're done. Continue to pair the change notifier.

docs.title: Pair the change notifier
docs.text:
Pairing gives the org a key it uses to sign notifications, and gives AlgoBridge a way to check them.

  1. Confirm the bundle is 1.1.0 with the remote site set to your PUBLIC_URL, and that the permission set is assigned.
  2. On the Change notifier card, click Pair notifier.

AlgoBridge sends the org a single-use code that expires in 10 minutes and is never shown. Salesforce calls AlgoBridge back once to collect the key. This costs two API requests, the pairing and a status check. You see Notifier paired. and the card shows Paired, key abk_…, no notification yet.

docs.title: Add the Flows
docs.text:
The notifier is driven by two record-triggered Flows on each synced object. Add them by hand for every object you map.

Flow 1: saves

  1. In Setup → Flows, create a Record-Triggered Flow on the object.
  2. Trigger it when A record is created or updated, with no entry conditions.
  3. Optimize it for Actions and Related Records.
  4. Add an Action and pick AlgoBridge: Notify Change (category AlgoBridge).
  5. Set its input records to {!$Record}.
  6. Save it with the label AlgoBridge notify <Object> save and the API name algobridge_notify_<Object>_save.
  7. Activate it.

Flow 2: deletes

Repeat the steps with the trigger A record is deleted, the label AlgoBridge notify <Object> delete and the API name algobridge_notify_<Object>_delete.

API names for custom objects

Flow API names can't contain a double underscore, so write Invoice__c as Invoice_c: algobridge_notify_Invoice_c_save.

A Flow on an object you don't sync is harmless: AlgoBridge ignores the notification. Object names match regardless of case.

docs.title: Select the change notifier
docs.text:
1. Click Use this source on the Change notifier card.
  2. AlgoBridge checks the notifier is installed and paired, that PUBLIC_URL uses https, and that it holds a live key.
  3. Save a record on a synced object in Salesforce. The card's last notification time updates and the change arrives in PostgreSQL.

You can watch notifier_notification_accepted events in the Live log.

docs.title: Rotate or revoke the key
docs.text:
• Rotate key issues a new key for two API requests. The old key keeps working for 24 hours, so in-flight notifications aren't lost. Rotate on a schedule.
  • Revoke deletes every key, with no API request. Salesforce keeps sending, and each send is refused until you pair again. Sync falls back to polling. Repeated refusals open the notifier_auth_failures alert.

If a key may have leaked

Click Revoke, then Pair notifier. Don't use Rotate key: it keeps the old key working for 24 hours.

Disconnecting Salesforce deletes the keys, so pair again after you connect. A reconnect to the same org keeps them.

docs.title: Know the limits
docs.text:
• Saves by the integration user aren't notified. If you reconnect as a different user, pair again.
  • Undelete, merge, cascade delete and deactivated Flows send nothing. The hourly fallback poll and the daily reconciliation sweep catch these.
  • Nothing is sent from batch or future contexts.
  • Each notification is one asynchronous Apex call, from the org's daily allowance and from the transaction's limit of 50 future calls, which your own code shares. The action skips sending when less than 1% of the daily allowance is left.
  • Sends are fire and forget with a 10 second timeout. A missed send is caught by the fallback poll.

docs.title: Remove the bundle
docs.text:
1. Deactivate and delete the AlgoBridge Flows.
  2. Click Revoke on the Change notifier card.
  3. Switch the change source to Composite polling.
  4. In Salesforce, delete the bundle's classes, the custom setting, the remote site setting and the permission set.

If you skip step 3, the daily check marks the source unavailable and polling falls back to Composite.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Deploy failed

The panel shows the deploy error. The usual causes are a missing Author Apex or Modify Metadata permission on the integration user, or a failing test in the org. Fix the cause and click Deploy bundle again.

A bundle deploy is already running.

A deploy is in progress. Wait for it to finish.

The Apex bundle in the org has no notifier.

The org has a bundle older than 1.1.0. Deploy the bundle, then pair again.

Salesforce refused the pairing.

The AlgoBridge Integration permission set isn't assigned to the integration user, or the remote site setting doesn't cover your PUBLIC_URL. Pairing is also limited to 5 attempts a minute: if you hit the limit, wait a minute. Nothing changed, so fix the cause and pair again.

Notifier paired, but the follow-up status check found a problem.

The pairing worked but the status call found an issue. The Change notifier card shows it once the notifier is the selected source, and selecting it checks again.

Notifications stop arriving

Check that the Flows are active, that PUBLIC_URL and the remote site still match, and look for notifier_notification_rejected in the Live log. If the log reports notifier_key_unreadable, pair again.
